summary:
Metropolitana is the region of best and worst in the country compressed into one administrative unit. Ñuñoa approved the first municipal anti-discrimination ordinance in Chile that explicitly prohibits hate speech, obliges non-discrimination clauses in municipal tenders and contracts, creates a communal seal for good practice, and requires anti-exclusion notices in municipal buildings — a genuinely first-in-country institutional protection for a visitor in that commune. Vitacura's mayor declined to raise the LGBT pride flag on 17 May after a rebellion by Republican councillors, despite a prior commitment to Movilh. The ADM1 unit's internal spread (Ñuñoa vs Vitacura) is larger than most regions' entire deviation from the national score.

Metropolitana held 25.12 % of national cases in 2024 (second only to Valparaíso), but as the country's most populous region this share is roughly proportional. In 2025, Metropolitana was one of only two regions where recorded cases fell. The unit carries the strongest institutional depth in Chile: national-level courts, the largest civil-society infrastructure, the greatest concentration of trans and non-binary community resources, and the highest density of legal aid and complaint mechanisms available to a visitor who encounters discrimination.

Against the national 0.72, this is a +0.02 deviation, the only positive unit score. The Ñuñoa ordinance and the falling case count edge the region slightly above national; the Vitacura episode and the 25 % share pull the other way but are offset by proportional population. Compared with Valparaíso (0.56), the +0.18 gap reflects that Santiago, despite carrying a quarter of national cases, has the institutional machinery to respond, while Valparaíso's problem is density of incidents without equivalent counterweight.

sources.summary: Movilh press release (15 April 2026): Ñuñoa's municipal council, led by Mayor Sebastián Sichel, approved the country's first anti-discrimination ordinance that explicitly prohibits hate speech (9 votes to 1, one governing-party councillor against); it was drafted with Movilh by the commune's Diversity and Non-Discrimination department, obliges non-discrimination clauses in municipal tenders and contracts, creates a communal seal recognising good practice, and requires anti-exclusion notices in municipal buildings.

NOTE: page not retrievable at research time (fetch blocked); the underlying health-sector-adjacent news site (The Clinic) report covers the Vitacura municipality's decision not to fly the LGBT pride flag around 17 May 2025 after Republican councillors rebelled, despite a prior commitment to Movilh.

Movilh's XXIII annual report on human rights and sexual/gender diversity ('Hechos 2024', March 2025; PDF partially retrieved at fetch time): the yearly tally of homo/transphobia cases and complaints by region behind the recorded shares used here - Metropolitana second nationally at 25.12% of 2024 cases, behind Valparaiso - with category breakdowns and year-on-year change.

tangentialFactors: Much of the recorded-case load and the flag dispute concerns sexual-orientation and general visibility conflicts (public rainbow symbols, hate-speech counts covering gay and lesbian people) rather than gender identity specifically - relevant to how a visibly queer-presenting visitor reads the two communes' climates.
localsOnly: Protective depth concentrates in resident-facing machinery - municipal tender clauses, communal seals, the region's share of legal-aid and complaint bodies - which a visitor can use only if they stay long enough to file; likewise the ordinance's educational and health-programme provisions.
